messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Viktor is a 60-year-old man of Eastern European descent who works the early shift at a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of the city, where he has lived with his long-term partner for the past eleven years. He was referred for psychological assessment following a visit to his primary care physician, who noted elevated scores on a routine screening questionnaire and a marked deterioration in Viktor's functioning over recent months. His PCL-5 score of 62 places him firmly in the severe range, and the picture that has emerged across the intake and first two sessions is one of a man quietly consumed by something he has never been able to put into words.

The precipitating event occurred decades ago during Viktor's military service, in a close-quarters engagement in which several members of his unit were killed. Viktor was one of a small number who survived, and the specific circumstances of that survival — the position he happened to occupy, the decision he made in the seconds before the worst of it — have never left him. He walked away. Others did not. In the years immediately following his discharge he managed, as many do, through a combination of forward momentum and deliberate not-looking. He built a life, found a partner, took the warehouse job, and told himself that what had happened was behind him.

It was not. When Viktor tries to recall the event — and sometimes the recall comes without invitation — what surfaces is not a coherent narrative but something more like a wall of sensation: the particular weight of the uniform he was wearing, the smell of the air, and then a terror so immediate and physical that it is indistinguishable from the original moment. He has told his partner almost nothing, in part because he genuinely cannot find the language. He knows what happened. He knows the sequence of events. But when he opens his mouth, the words simply are not there, and the failure to articulate it has quietly reinforced his conviction that what he carries is unspeakable — something outside the range of normal human experience, something that marks him as permanently altered. These qualities of the memory itself — its vividness, its wordlessness, its capacity to return him bodily to that day — have deepened his belief that the world remains fundamentally dangerous, that threat is always proximate, and that he survived something he had no right to survive.

It is this last conviction that sits at the centre of Viktor's presentation. He feels guilty for being alive. He has come to believe, with a quiet certainty that resists challenge, that his survival was a kind of theft — that something was taken from the men who died and given, undeservedly, to him. This survival guilt has corroded his sense of who he is; he no longer recognises the person he was before, and the man he sees now feels like an impostor wearing borrowed time. These appraisals have driven him toward a set of strategies that feel, to Viktor, like the only rational response to an intolerable situation. He avoids thinking about the event with a vigilance that costs him considerable mental energy. He has not returned to the neighbourhood where his old barracks were located, even when a route through that area would have been convenient. And in a detail that struck his clinician as particularly telling, he stopped wearing a particular style of heavy work jacket — one that, in cut and colour, resembled the uniform from that day — despite the cold of the warehouse floor.

The avoidance has not protected him. If anything, the years of not-thinking have kept the memory raw and unprocessed, so that when it does surface it retains its full original terror, which in turn confirms his belief that he is fundamentally changed and that the world is a place where catastrophe waits. His partner has noticed his withdrawal and has stopped asking questions, and Viktor has interpreted this as further evidence that he is now someone unknowable — even to the person closest to him.

What finally brought him in was a moment at work, three months ago, when a younger colleague arrived wearing a jacket that stopped Viktor cold in the middle of the loading bay. He stood there, unable to move, certain for several seconds that he was back. He has not told anyone what happened in those seconds. What he is most afraid of, he said quietly at the end of the second session, is that there is no longer a version of himself worth recovering.
